text.p: Greece's belt-tightening 1997 budget was passed by parliament on Sunday and socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis said its tough measures were the only way to prepare the economy for a single European currency.
"The budget aims for a strong Greece. A Greece with a strong voice in the European Union. There is no alternative to this budget," he told parliament shortly before the vote.
The budget, described by the socialists as the toughest in 15 years, passed by 160 votes to 136 with four absent in the 300-seat parliament.
Simitis said that cutting large deficits was his priority and "everyone must make sacrifices, especially the wealthy" to ensure the economy was ready for a single European currency.
He has said that he wants Greece to enter European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 2001. The more powerful EU countries aim to forge EMU and a single currency in 1999.
Simitis said that failure to achieve economic integration with Greece's European Union partners would lead to isolation and a national disaster.
"We will take all necessary measures, we will implement all necessary proposals so that Greece responds to the challange of the European Union," he said.
His economic plan is aimed at cutting the budget deficit to 4.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from 7.6 percent in 1996.
It counts largely on economic growth and raising revenues by adding new taxes, hiking existing taxes and eliminating tax breaks. But it also sets limits on state spending.
In his address, Simitis called again on farmers, who have blockaded the nation's roads for 24 days, to free the highways and start talks on their problems with the government.
"I hope that after today's vote all roads will be free. We never said 'no' to a dialogue but dialogue cannot be imposed with autocratic and extreme methods," he said.
Farmers in Thessaly, heartland of the revolt, tightened the blockade on Saturday which has cut the main north-south highway, causing Christmas transport woes and heavy economic damage.

The Thessaly farmers' committee later began talks on whether to suspend their action, apparently under pressure after farmers in the northern Macedonia and Thrace regions, and at the western port of Patras, lifted their blockades.

The Thessaly farmers continued talking on Sunday, with some indications the committee wanted to suspend the blockade but was unsure how the decision would go down with the rank-and-file on the barricades.
Thessaly farmers have set up tent cities on the north-south highway linking Athens to the country's second city of Salonika, vowing not to budge until their demands were met.
They want cheaper fuel, higher price supports and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled. Simitis has rejected the demands, saying the government has no more money to give.
Simitis, elected on pledges of economic reform in September, received a much-needed boost on Friday when seamen suspended a five-day strike which has caused transport chaos at the ports.
They suspended the strike until January 8, and said they expected the government to meet their terms over tax breaks and pension funds in the meantime.
